source: Cornell University NYS IPM Program / USDA APHIS PPQ National Late Blight Forecasting Network (USAblight)
title: Potato Late Blight (Phytophthora infestans, Oomycota Peronosporaceae) - Irish Potato Famine Pathogen
content: Potato late blight, caused by the heterothallic, hemibiotrophic oomycete Phytophthora infestans (Mont.) de Bary (phylum Oomycota, order Peronosporales, family Peronosporaceae, kingdom Stramenopiles, SAR supergroup) is historically the most notorious and agriculturally devastating plant disease in modern human history. It was the causal agent of the Great Irish Potato Famine (Gorta Mor / Great Hunger) of 1845-1851, which caused the death by starvation and disease of approximately 1.1 million people in Ireland, the emigration of an additional 1.5-2 million Irish people to the United States, Canada, Australia, and Britain, and the permanent sociopolitical, demographic, and economic transformation of an entire island nation. Today, late blight remains the single most destructive and economically costly disease of cultivated potato (Solanum tuberosum L.) and tomato (Solanum lycopersicum L.) worldwide, occurring in every major potato- and tomato-growing region of the globe. Annual global economic costs of potato late blight (direct yield losses + cost of fungicide applications + post-harvest storage losses) are estimated at US$ 6.7-10.0 billion (2023 USD); approximately 10-15% of the entire global potato fungicide expenditure (approximately $1-3 billion annually) is targeted specifically at late blight control. Yield losses of 50-100% can occur in unsprayed susceptible potato cultivars within 2-3 weeks under ideal cool, wet, late-blight-favorable weather conditions; even with the most intensive state-of-the-art fungicide programs in developed-country commercial production, late blight still consistently causes 5-15% annual potato and tomato yield losses. The pathogen has a very narrow primary host range, confined almost exclusively to the genus Solanum section Petota (potatoes) and section Lycopersicum (tomatoes), but can also naturally infect cultivated eggplant (Solanum melongena, rarely), pepino (S. muricatum), and approximately 200+ wild Solanum species, including the important agricultural weeds horsenettle (S. carolinense), bittersweet nightshade (S. dulcamara), black nightshade (S. nigrum), hairy nightshade (S. sarrachoides, S. physalifolium), and jimsonweed (Datura stramonium, rarely, under experimental inoculation). Late blight attacks all above-ground green plant parts (leaves, stems, petioles, inflorescences, pedicels, green tomato fruit), as well as below-ground potato tubers; it does not infect true potato seed (TPS) or mature, dormant tomato seed. The diagnostic symptoms of late blight on potato and tomato foliage are distinctive and different from early blight (Alternaria solani). On potato leaves, the first visible lesions typically appear on the lower (basal) canopy or in the upper canopy after extended wet periods: small, irregular to circular, dark green to black, water-soaked ('greasy') necrotic lesions 5-20 mm in diameter, usually located at or near the leaf tip and margins where water droplets collect. Under humid, cool (16-22 C) conditions, these lesions expand rapidly (2-5 cm per day) into large, dark brown to black, irregularly shaped blighted areas with a faint, pale yellow-green chlorotic 'water-soaked' border or halo at the lesion edge; the 'greasy' or 'water-soaked' appearance of the lesion margin is the most important diagnostic feature distinguishing late blight from early blight (which has dry, target-zonate lesions with sharp margins). Under high-humidity conditions (RH > 90%, still air, cool nights, dewy mornings), diagnostic thin, delicate, white-to-grayish, downy, felt-like sporangiophores and lemon-shaped sporangia (the 'sporulating lesion' stage) appear on the LOWER (abaxial) leaf surface directly beneath the necrotic lesion (this white downy sporulation is best observed in the early morning with a 10x hand lens on leaves collected while still dewy). Late blight leaf lesions are not zonate (no target-board rings), unlike early blight; they turn brittle, papery, and light brown when dry, but when held under a moist plastic bag for 24-48 hours at room temperature will produce the characteristic white sporulation on the lower surface (this is the 'moist chamber incubation' diagnostic field test). On potato and tomato stems, petioles, and pedicels, late blight lesions are elongated, dark brown to black, slightly sunken, water-soaked stem cankers 1-10 cm long; under humid conditions, white downy sporangiophores and sporangia emerge in a ring around the stem canker. Severe stem girdling cankers near the soil line ('collar rot' or 'late blight black leg') will cause rapid wilting, collapse, and death of entire potato or tomato vines. On green and ripe tomato fruit, late blight produces irregularly shaped, slightly sunken, grayish-brown to dark brown, firm, leathery, 'greasy-appearing' lesions (5-50 mm) that expand rapidly and often develop white downy sporulation (P. infestans sporangia) on the fruit surface under humid conditions; entire tomato fruit clusters can rot within 3-5 days. On potato tubers, infection occurs when sporangia and zoospores are washed from blighted leaves and vine debris down through the soil profile (during rain or overhead irrigation) and come in contact with developing daughter tubers; tuber lesions are slightly depressed, irregular, dark reddish-brown to purple-brown discolorations of the tuber skin 10-60 mm across; when cut transversely, the underlying tuber flesh shows a characteristic shallow (3-15 mm deep), firm, dry, granular, reddish-brown to copper-colored necrotic 'marbling' or 'granulation' in the outer perimedullary cortex region immediately beneath the periderm (this reddish-brown granulation distinguishes late blight tuber rot from Erwinia bacterial soft rot [watery, mushy, smelly], early blight tuber rot [darker brown, dry, sharply defined corky lesion], Fusarium dry rot [cavities lined with white, pink, or orange mycelium], and Rhizoctonia black scurf [superficial black sclerotia on skin surface only]). Secondary infection by soft-rot Pectobacterium and Erwinia bacteria commonly enters through late blight tuber lesions and causes mushy, foul-smelling wet tuber rot in both the field and in storage, often leading to complete breakdown of entire potato storage piles within 2-4 months. Phytophthora infestans is a heterothallic oomycete with two mating types, designated A1 and A2; sexual reproduction (and the production of thick-walled, long-lived, diploid, soil-borne overwintering oospores, 24-35 um diameter, yellowish-brown) occurs only when mycelia of both compatible A1 and A2 mating types grow together in the same plant tissue. Historically (from 1845 through the early 1980s), only the A1 mating type of P. infestans was present outside of its center of origin in the Toluca Valley, central Mexico, and therefore sexual reproduction and oospore formation did not occur; the pathogen survived the winter / off-season almost exclusively as mycelium in infected, living, dormant potato seed tubers (seed-piece borne inoculum) and as mycelium in infected volunteer ('ground-keeper') potato tubers that overwintered in soil and sprouted the following spring. A second global migration event during the late 1970s and early 1980s introduced the A2 mating type into Europe and then to North America, South America, Africa, and Asia via contaminated seed potato shipments; today, both A1 and A2 mating types coexist in most major potato-growing regions worldwide, and sexual reproduction (oospores) is now documented in > 40 countries, greatly complicating disease management because oospores can survive in soil and crop debris for 3-7 years in the absence of any living potato or tomato host, providing a potent new soil-borne source of primary inoculum independent of seed tubers. The asexual polycyclic infection cycle, which is responsible for almost all of the explosive mid- and late-season epidemic spread, proceeds as follows: (1) primary inoculum arises in spring from three possible sources: (a) infected potato seed tubers (the most important primary inoculum source in most regions historically) - when an infected seed tuber sprouts, a small proportion of sprouts develop systemic late blight infection and emerge from the soil as a sporulating 'primary focus' or 'source plant' that produces sporangia; (b) oospores germinating in the soil (now important in regions where both mating types occur) produce sporangia that release zoospores that infect the lower leaves and underground parts of young potato sprouts; (c) infected volunteer potato plants (ground keepers) and wild Solanum weed hosts that overwinter in mild-climate regions. (2) Asexual sporangia (20-35 x 15-25 um, lemon-shaped, deciduous, with a distinct apical papilla 3-5 um wide, borne on sympodially branched sporangiophores with swollen, club-shaped, 90-degree-bent pedicel attachment points) are produced abundantly on the lower surface of sporulating lesions during humid nights at 16-22 C. (3) Sporangia are dispersed primarily by turbulent wind (can travel 50-100 km downwind from a source under storm conditions; typical within-field and between-field dispersal is 10-500 m) and secondarily by rain splash. (4) Infection occurs via two distinct pathways depending on temperature: (a) at relatively cool temperatures of 10-18 C, sporangia germinate indirectly within 30-90 minutes by releasing 6-12 (typically 8) biflagellate motile kidney-shaped zoospores (8-12 x 6-9 um) that swim in free water films on the leaf surface, encyst on stomata or the cuticle, produce a short germ tube, and penetrate the host directly through the cuticle or through stomatal openings. (b) at warmer temperatures of 19-26 C, sporangia may germinate directly by producing a single germ tube that penetrates via appressorium. Infection requires at least 4-6 hours of continuous free moisture on the leaf surface from dew, fog, or rain at temperatures of 10-26 C; the latent period (infection to first visible sporulating lesion) is 4-14 days depending on temperature (optimum 5-7 days at 18-22 C). Under ideal weather conditions, each lesion produces up to 300,000 sporangia per day for 5-10 days, and thus late blight epidemics exhibit classic exponential 'compound interest' logistic growth, potentially increasing from 1 lesion per 100,000 plants to 100% crop blighted in as little as 14-21 days. Management of potato and tomato late blight is one of the most complex and intensively studied areas of all plant pathology; an integrated, multi-component approach is mandatory. (1) Exclusion and regulatory measures are the first line of defense: plant only certified, government-inspected, late-blight-indexed potato seed tubers produced in low-disease-pressure arid seed-increase zones (this eliminates the #1 source of primary inoculum in most regions); follow all national and international seed potato quarantine regulations (USDA APHIS, EU Plant Health Directive, NPPO requirements) preventing movement of untested seed potatoes; plant only certified disease-free tomato transplants produced in screened, soilless transplant houses with no late blight history; do not plant saved 'home-saved' potato tubers or tomato seed from a late-blight-affected crop as primary inoculum sources. (2) Cultural practices: (a) eliminate all overwintering inoculum sources before planting: destroy all volunteer potato plants (ground keepers) growing in or near potato and tomato fields by disking, herbicide application, or hand removal in early spring; remove wild Solanum weed reservoirs (Solanum dulcamara, S. nigrum, S. sarrachoides, S. carolinense) from field borders, irrigation ditches, fence rows, and transplant production facilities; (b) cull and destroy (hot-compost, landfill, or bury > 1 m deep) all visibly infected potato seed pieces and seed tubers at planting time; (c) use hilled-up rows, well-drained soils, and raised beds to minimize tuber contact with sporangia-laden surface water; (d) use wide plant spacing, open-canopy planting patterns, avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization (promotes lush succulent susceptible growth), and orient planting rows parallel to prevailing winds to maximize air movement and accelerate canopy drying; (e) avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation wherever practical, especially during late evening and overnight hours which extend leaf wetness periods; use furrow, drip, or subsurface irrigation; (f) when late blight is first detected in a small area of a field, remove and destroy (burn, bury) all visibly infected plants ('roguing' or 'removal of foci') and immediately apply a curative fungicide treatment to the entire surrounding 50 m buffer zone; (g) implement a 'vine-kill' program 2-3 weeks prior to mechanical harvest by applying desiccants (diquat, paraquat, carfentrazone) or using mechanical flailing or undercutting to kill potato vines before harvest; this prevents sporulating late blight lesions on vines from depositing sporangia onto the soil surface where they can infect daughter tubers during the digging operation. (3) Predictive forecasting / decision-support systems are mandatory for economical, environmentally responsible late blight control. The most widely used models (BLITECAST, SimCast, LATEBLIGHT, WISDOM, USAblight, IBLIGHT, EuroBlight) calculate daily risk values from real-time meteorological data (air temperature, relative humidity, rainfall duration, leaf wetness duration, wind speed) and schedule fungicide applications only when late-blight-favorable weather (infection periods) are predicted. Forecasting systems typically reduce fungicide use by 30-60% compared to rigid calendar-based 7-day protectant schedules while maintaining equivalent or better late blight control. (4) Genetic resistance is the most promising, sustainable, long-term late blight management strategy. Two complementary classes of genetic resistance exist in Solanum spp.: (a) Major, dominant, race-specific vertical (R) resistance genes (Rpi = Resistance to P. infestans), originally identified in the Mexican hexaploid wild potato species Solanum demissum (R1-R11 genes); > 60 new Rpi genes have now been characterized from > 20 different wild Solanum species (S. bulbocastanum, S. venturii, S. stoloniferum, S. verrucosum, S. microdontum, S. paucissectum, S. chacoense, S. jamesii, S. schenckii). R genes typically confer near-complete immunity to specific races of P. infestans carrying the matching Avirulence (Avr) effector gene, but are frequently overcome by new virulent P. infestans races in 3-10 years due to pathogen evolution and strong selection pressure from monogenic deployment. (b) Quantitative, partial, horizontal (field) polygenic resistance (QR), typically mediated by multiple QTLs (quantitative trait loci) with minor individual effects, reduces but does not eliminate infection, lesion expansion rate, and sporulation capacity; QR is generally race-nonspecific and considered more durable over time. Cultivars combining stacked (pyramided) multiple Rpi genes (via marker-assisted breeding and cisgenic/transgenic approaches) with high levels of polygenic QR are the current industry breeding goal. Late-blight-resistant commercial potato cultivars currently available include: 'Defender' (Rpi-blb2 + QR), 'Jacqueline Lee' (R1 + QR), 'Altaros', 'Bionica', 'Toluca' (Rpi-blb1 + Rpi-blb2), 'Sarpo Mira', 'Sarpo Axona' (R3a + R3b + multiple QTLs - extremely high resistance to all known EU races), 'Yukon Gem' (Rpi-sto1), 'Palisade Russet' (moderate QR). A landmark 2014 landmark cisgenic 'potato late blight resistant' event (developed by Wageningen UR and the Sainsbury Laboratory) stacking three Rpi genes ('Rpi-sto1, Rpi-vnt1.1, Rpi-blb3') has shown > 99% late blight resistance across 4 years of EU field trials with zero fungicide input. In tomato, major genes Ph-1, Ph-2, Ph-3, Ph-4, Ph-5 from S. pimpinellifolium and S. habrochaites provide varying levels of late blight resistance; 'Mountain Merit', 'Iron Lady', 'Defiant PhR', 'Jasper', 'Matt's Wild Cherry' combine multiple Ph genes with good agronomic traits. (5) Chemical fungicide programs are the primary late blight control tool in most commercial potato and tomato production. The most important fungicide groups for late blight (all target the oomycete, Stramenopile-specific biochemical pathways, and are ineffective against ascomycete/basidiomycete fungi; note that FRAC codes for downy mildews / oomycetes are different from ascomycete fungicides) are: FRAC 4 (Phenylamides = PA: mefenoxam = metalaxyl-M, metalaxyl, benalaxyl, ofurace, oxadixyl. PA was the most active systemic curative material ever developed for late blight, with up to 14 days kickback curative activity; however, PA resistance is extremely widespread in P. infestans globally (resistance factor RF > 100, all A2-mating-type US-8, US-22, US-23, US-24 genotypes are resistant; only rare A1-mating-type lineages are still sensitive). PA is still used but always tank-mixed with a multi-site contact and used at maximum 2-3 applications per season; use only on crops where resistance monitoring confirms PA-sensitive P. infestans populations. FRAC 40 (Carboxylic Acid Amides = CAA: dimethomorph, mandipropamid, iprovalicarb, benthiavalicarb-isopropyl, valifenalate, pyrimorph. Protectant + 1-3 day kickback curative activity. Excellent activity; CAA resistance has developed in some P. infestans populations in China, the Netherlands, and Belgium (G1105S mutation in CesA3 cellulose synthase gene). Always tank-mix with multi-site partner; limit 4 applications per year; do not apply consecutively more than 2 times. FRAC 45 (QoI anti-oomycete = QoI-AO, FRAC formerly 21: famoxadone, fenamidone. Protectant only; cross-resistant with FRAC 11 QoI via Cyt b G143A mutation. Not recommended for sole use due to widespread QoI resistance risk). FRAC U8 (Mitochondrial respiration inhibitor: ametoctradin. FRAC 45-like activity; protectant; new mode of action, low resistance risk so far). FRAC 49 (Oxysterol-binding protein inhibitor = OSBPI: oxathiapiprolin. The newest, most potent, and most active single-site late blight fungicide ever developed; extremely low use rates (10-25 g ai/ha); up to 21 days protectant + 3-5 day excellent curative kickback; locally systemic and translaminar; excellent movement within potato canopy. Low resistance risk so far; always use with multi-site partner and alternate with non-FRAC 49 modes). FRAC P07 (Phosphonates / Phosphorous acid: fosetyl-Al, potassium phosphite, phosphorous acid. FRAC 33; multi-site, systemic, stimulates host induced defense response; moderate protectant + mild curative activity; no resistance reported after > 35 years of widespread use; permitted in many organic production systems as potassium phosphite). FRAC 28 (CAA-like, benthiavalicarb variant: benthiavalicarb-isopropyl). FRAC 22 (Benzamides: zoxamide; protectant, anti-oomycete tubulin inhibitor; very low resistance risk; useful partner). Multi-site contact protectant materials with zero resistance risk (the backbone of every late blight fungicide program): FRAC M3 (dithiocarbamates: mancozeb, maneb, metiram, zineb, thiram - the gold standard protectant, always full-rate tank-mix partner with every single-site), FRAC M1 (fixed coppers: Bordeaux mixture, copper hydroxide, copper oxychloride, tribasic copper sulfate - extremely important protectant and curative in organic systems; has some anti-late-blight activity even with 1-2 day kickback when applied properly), FRAC M2 (elemental sulfur: weak anti-late-blight activity alone; adequate as a component of organic tank-mix). All fungicide programs must strictly follow EuroBlight / USAblight / FRAC anti-resistance guidelines: (a) never use any single-site anti-oomycete fungicide SOLO (alone); always tank-mix with a full recommended rate of FRAC M3 or FRAC M1 multi-site partner to prevent resistance. (b) Maximum 2-3 consecutive applications of any single FRAC mode of action group before switching to a different group; never back-to-back applications of the same single-site group. (c) Limit total seasonal applications of any high-resistance-risk group (FRAC 4, FRAC 40, FRAC 49, FRAC 11/QoI) to 3-4 per growing season maximum. (d) Initiate fungicide sprays BEFORE symptoms appear, based on forecasting model infection risk signals; do not wait for visible lesions to appear (especially for oomycete pathogens, by the time visible lesions appear, thousands of sporangia have already been produced and spread within a field). (e) Apply fungicides with high-volume, air-assist spray equipment (ultra-low-volume electrostatic sprayers for potatoes) with appropriate adjuvants (spreader-stickers, nonionic surfactants) to achieve maximum coverage on the lower (abaxial) leaf surface where infection occurs, especially in dense potato canopies. (6) Organic late blight control programs rely almost exclusively on: (a) resistant cultivars; (b) strict cultural measures (early planting, early harvest, avoiding overhead irrigation, wide spacing, volunteer/wild-host eradication, prompt vine kill); (c) Bordeaux mixture (copper sulfate + hydrated lime, formulated as 10:10:100 or 12:12:100) applied every 7-10 days on a strict protectant schedule before infection risk; (d) fixed coppers (copper hydroxide, copper oxychloride, copper ammonium complexes) at metallic copper rates of 1-2 kg/ha per application; (e) potassium phosphonate (phosphorous acid) sprays for mild systemic kickback activity; (f) microbial biological control agents (Bacillus amyloliquefaciens QST 713 / Serenade ASO, B. subtilis GB03, Streptomyces lydicus WYEC 108, Pseudomonas fluorescens A506, Trichoderma harzianum T-22, Reynoutria sachalinensis (giant knotweed) extract / Regalia). Organic programs typically require 10-15 sprays per season and achieve 60-85% control under moderate late blight pressure, but are usually not economically sufficient under severe late blight epidemic years with highly susceptible cultivars unless combined with resistant cultivar genetics. (7) Post-harvest storage management: do not place visibly late-blight-affected tubers into storage; pre-grade and remove all blighted and damaged tubers before storage; cure tubers at 10-13 C and 95% RH for 10-14 days to promote periderm suberization and wound healing, followed by rapid cooling to 3-6 C for long-term storage; maintain good air circulation and uniform temperature distribution in storage piles to prevent condensation on tuber surfaces; monitor stored tubers frequently (at least monthly) for any development of late blight tuber rot and secondary soft rot expansion.
